issues.legal_issue: A civil court may determine whether the jurisdictional fact required for a statutory officer’s exclusive inquiry exists, and may question determinations beyond the limits of that inquiry.
material_facts: The Settlement Officer found that the village was not an inam estate under the then-applicable definition, but also found that it had become an estate under a separate amendment.
The landholders brought a civil suit asserting that the village was not an inam village because the grant did not cover the whole village.
The civil court decree on that issue became final, and the parties to a related rent-or-damages suit agreed to abide by its outcome.
issues.conclusion: The civil court had jurisdiction to decide whether the village was an inam village; the Settlement Officer’s finding on that jurisdictional fact was not final, and an unnecessary or incidental determination beyond the statutory inquiry could also be questioned in civil court.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 9 CPC, civil courts have jurisdiction over civil suits unless it is expressly or impliedly excluded. Section 9(1) of the Madras Estates (Abolition and Conversion into Ryotwari) Act, 1948 gave the Settlement Officer exclusive jurisdiction to determine whether an inam village was an inam estate, but the existence of an inam village was a preliminary jurisdictional fact and was not left finally to that officer. A finding on that fact could be questioned in an ordinary civil proceeding, and res judicata did not bar its adjudication by a competent court. The Court followed Addanki Tiruvenkata Tata Desika Charyulu v. State of Andhra Pradesh, AIR 1964 SC 807, and referred to District Board, Tanjore v. Noor Mohammed, (1952) 2 M.J. 586 (S.C.); it also noted Gosukonda Venkata Narasayya v. State of Madras as approved in Addanki.

predicates.civil_suit_challenges_statutory_classifi: A party brings a civil suit challenging a classification made in a statutory inquiry.
predicates.dispute_concerns_jurisdictional_fact: The dispute concerns a preliminary fact whose existence is required before the statutory officer may exercise exclusive jurisdiction.
predicates.officer_decided_beyond_assigned_inquiry: The statutory officer made a determination unnecessary or incidental to the inquiry assigned to that officer.

issues.definition: When a civil suit challenges a statutory classification and the dispute concerns a jurisdictional fact or a determination beyond the officer’s assigned inquiry, the civil court may determine the disputed issue.

issues.legal_issue: Amendments that alter substantive rights do not change the rights governing pending actions unless the legislation clearly makes that change retrospective.
material_facts: The civil suits were instituted before the 1957 amendments came into force and were still pending when those amendments commenced.
The amendments enlarged the definition relevant to the statutory scheme and changed the government’s right to appeal against a Settlement Officer’s decision.
The amendments contained no clear language making them apply to pending or concluded civil actions.
issues.conclusion: The 1957 amendments operated prospectively and did not alter the parties’ rights in the pending suits, which had to be decided under the law applicable when those actions were instituted.
issues.legal_principle: Ordinarily, substantive rights in a pending action are determined under the law in force when the action began unless the later legislation clearly expresses an intention to vary those rights. The Court applied that rule of statutory construction, noting that the 1957 amendments contained no express or necessarily implied retrospective operation and affected substantive rights and obligations.

rule.if: civil_action_pending_when_law_changed and (new_law_changes_substantive_rights or new_law_imposes_new_obligations) and not law_clearly_makes_change_retroactive

predicates.civil_action_pending_when_law_changed: A civil action was pending when a later law came into force.
predicates.new_law_changes_substantive_rights: The later law changes substantive rights relevant to the pending action.
predicates.new_law_imposes_new_obligations: The later law imposes obligations or disabilities relevant to the pending action.
predicates.law_clearly_makes_change_retroactive: The later law clearly states, expressly or by necessary implication, that the change applies retrospectively.

issues.definition: If an action is pending when a law changing substantive rights or imposing new obligations comes into force, and the law does not clearly make that change retrospective, the pending claims remain governed by the prior law.

issues.legal_issue: A lawful agreement to abide by the determination of an issue in another pending case may be recorded as a consent decree, whose agreed portion is final and binding between the parties.
material_facts: In a civil suit for rent or damages, the parties agreed to abide by the final determination in another pending case of the common issue whether the village was an estate.
The State was contesting that issue in the other case, safeguarding the respondents’ interests there.
The court recorded the agreement in a decree, and the later appeal in substance concerned the extent of the land and the amount recoverable, not the agreed portion of the decree.
issues.conclusion: The agreement was lawful, and the portion of the decree made in its terms was final and binding between the parties and was not appealable as a consent decree.
issues.legal_principle: Order 23 Rule 3 CPC permits a lawful partial compromise or adjustment of a suit and requires the court to record it and pass a decree to that extent. Section 96(3) CPC bars an appeal from a consent decree, reflecting the estoppel arising when parties accept a decree on agreed terms. Parties may lawfully agree to abide by the determination of the same issue in another pending case; such an arrangement is not, on these facts, collusive or an attempt to contract out of the law. The Court relied on Raja Sri Sailendra Narayan Bhanja Deo v. State of Orissa, [1956] SCR 72, Shri Prithvi Cotton Mills Ltd. v. Broach Borough Municipality, [1970] 1 SCR 388, and Reid v. Reid, (1886) 31 Ch. D. 403 at 408.

predicates.appeal_concerns_decree_in_civil_suit: An appeal is brought concerning a decree made in a civil suit.
predicates.parties_agreed_to_follow_result_in_relat: The parties agreed to abide by the determination of a common issue in another pending case.
predicates.court_recorded_agreement_in_decree: The court recorded the parties’ agreement in the decree.

issues.definition: When an appeal concerns a civil decree that records the parties’ agreement to follow the result in a related pending case, the agreed part of the decree is final and binding.

issues.legal_issue: A later amendment that applies retrospectively to certain statutory-officer decisions does not revive a decision already vacated by a final civil court decree unless the amendment clearly provides for that result.
material_facts: Before the 1960 amendment commenced, final civil court decrees had determined that the village was not an estate and had thereby vacated the Settlement Officer’s earlier decision on that issue.
The amendment addressed certain earlier decisions of Settlement Officers or tribunals, but did not expressly state that it revived decisions already vacated by civil court decrees.
The amendment did not specify a commencement date earlier than its publication.
issues.conclusion: The 1960 amendment applied only to decisions that were still subsisting at its commencement; it did not revive the Settlement Officer’s decision already vacated by the final civil court decrees or affect those decrees’ finality and binding effect.
issues.legal_principle: A legislature may alter the basis of a court’s decision, but merely declaring a decision non-binding is not enough to reverse it; the conditions on which the decision rests must be fundamentally altered. Even where legislation has some retrospective operation, it should not be read to interfere with vested rights more than its plain words require. Section 9-A of the Madras Estates (Abolition and Conversion into Ryotwari) Act, 1948, as inserted by the 1960 amendment, covered decisions still subsisting at commencement and did not clearly revive decisions already vacated by competent court decrees. Section 64-A(2) remained relevant to the binding effect of civil court decisions. The Court relied on Shri Prithvi Cotton Mills Ltd. v. Broach Borough Municipality, [1970] 1 SCR 388, and Reid v. Reid, (1886) 31 Ch. D. 403 at 408.

predicates.civil_decree_preceded_later_amendment: A civil court decree was made before a later amendment came into force.
predicates.decree_vacated_officer_decision: The decree vacated the statutory officer’s decision on the matter.
predicates.amendment_clearly_revives_vacated_decisi: The amendment clearly provides that decisions already vacated by court decrees are revived.

issues.definition: If a prior civil decree vacated an officer’s decision and a later amendment does not clearly revive vacated decisions, the amendment does not revive that decision.
